brief.head: Africa next door
brief.text: Most Indians live in con­di­tions com­pa­ra­ble to sub-Saharan Africa, Amit Varma said. The peo­ple elites think of as chauf­feurs and do­mes­tic help are the real mid­dle class. {054-C03}

brief.head: English, the network
brief.text: Parents wanted English even when gov­ern­ment schools in­sisted on the ver­nac­u­lar, Ajay Shah said, be­cause it is India’s link lan­guage. “The most pow­er­ful net­work of India is English.” {054-C08}

brief.head: A hole in the heart
brief.text: Some peo­ple are elec­tri­cal en­gi­neers at work and me­dieval the rest of the time, Ajay Shah said. A full per­son brings gen­eral in­tel­li­gence to ev­ery­thing, dahi in­cluded. {054-C16}

brief.head: A thousand flowers
brief.text: Ajay Shah wants every IIT, IIM and NIT freed from New Delhi’s cen­tral con­trol, which makes them all alike, like pub­lic sec­tor banks. “We need a thou­sand flow­ers to bloom.” {054-C19}

brief.head: Act in haste
brief.text: A bias for ac­tion helps a cre­ator learn by doing, Amit Varma said. For a state wield­ing co­er­cive power, Ajay Shah ar­gued, it is the great­est enemy. {054-C21}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India’s broken classrooms
lead.head: Spend more, learn less

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 54

body: Almost ev­ery­one agrees India needs more: more pub­lic and phil­an­thropic money, more teach­ers, more schools. Ajay Shah said at the out­set that he hoped to leave lis­ten­ers with “a lit­tle more dis­quiet”.
Amit Varma put the al­ter­na­tive in a line. “It’s not about more, it’s about bet­ter,” he said. {054-C01}

The ev­i­dence of fail­ure is stark. In Aser’s 2022 sur­vey, Varma said, 57 per cent of chil­dren in class five could not read a class two text. Among 14 to 18-year-olds, half could not do class three di­vi­sion.

Pouring in money has not helped. Citing Karthik Muralidharan’s re­search, Varma said that spend­ing more on build­ings and toi­lets, on hir­ing “bet­ter” teach­ers, or on school bags and mid­day meals does noth­ing for learn­ing out­comes.
The trou­ble is in­cen­tives. A teacher works hard until made per­ma­nent, he said, and then stops show­ing up: ab­sen­teeism in gov­ern­ment schools is “sky high”.

Shah wants every de­bate to set two num­bers side by side: per pupil ex­pense, which has dou­bled and quadru­pled, and an out­come mea­sure such as Aser or PISA. “The first step of the jour­ney of change, of the road to change, is data,” he said. {054-C02}
## Parents vote with their feet

The poor have al­ready given their ver­dict. Shah said par­ents are choos­ing to pay per­haps Rs 4,000 a year for a bud­get pri­vate school rather than take a free gov­ern­ment school that spends around Rs 10,000 per pupil.

Varma’s an­swer is school vouch­ers, an idea he cred­ited to Milton Friedman: keep the pub­lic money, but let it fol­low the child to any school. “Don’t send it to the schools, give it to the par­ents,” he said. {054-C06}
Shah took a milder line. Leave gov­ern­ment schools as they are, he said, but spend the same on every child in India, which­ever school they at­tend.
## The school­ing para­dox

Then came a coun­ter­in­tu­itive turn. Shah called Lant Pritchett’s *Where Has All the Education Gone?* one of the most im­por­tant pa­pers in the his­tory of de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics. Across coun­tries and decades, it found the gain in growth from more school­ing “es­sen­tially zero”. {054-C09}

Shah of­fered three ex­pla­na­tions: failed im­ple­men­ta­tion, ed­u­ca­tion as mere sig­nalling, or a mis­taken idea of what ed­u­ca­tion is. Varma backed the third: schools, he said, are “a 19th cen­tury ma­chine de­signed to solve a prob­lem of the 21st cen­tury”.

Industrial school­ing, Shah ar­gued, nur­tures only con­sci­en­tious­ness. “The kids that take or­ders, the kids who will obey are the ones who will flour­ish in the in­dus­tri­alised ed­u­ca­tion sys­tem,” he said.
## Start at home

What mat­ters most, the hosts agreed, hap­pens be­fore school and out­side it. Shah cited James Heckman, whose re­search finds the best re­turns in early child­hood, from birth to three or five, es­pe­cially for dis­ad­van­taged chil­dren. {054-R12}
Much of that learn­ing comes from over­hear­ing adults talk about ideas with a rich vo­cab­u­lary, Shah said. Varma added that what is missed in those years can­not be made up later.
Parents, Shah ar­gued, should see school for what it is: “a day­care”, just as col­lege is “day­care for teenagers”.
He urged the young to shun cre­den­tial­ism, pol­i­cy­mak­ers to be scep­ti­cal of ed­u­ca­tion spend­ing and com­pet­i­tive exams, and phi­lan­thropists to fund data and re­search, as with Aser.
Varma summed up what any learner, of any age, needs. “The key skill in mod­ern times is learn­ing how to learn,” he said.

second.label: Literacy and wealth
second.head: A report card for Nehru
second.deck: Ajay Shah imagines telling Jawaharlal Nehru what seventy-five per cent literacy bought India

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Nehru in a time machine

body: Jawaharlal Nehru’s gen­er­a­tion looked at Britain, with its schools and its Oxford and Cambridge, and saw ed­u­ca­tion as cen­tral to de­vel­op­ment. At in­de­pen­dence, Ajay Shah said, fe­male lit­er­acy in India was about 6 per cent. {#literacy6}

So Shah imag­ined going back to Nehru in a time ma­chine and telling him that by 2024 India had about 75 per cent lit­er­acy. Nehru, he said, would as­sume India must be at 60 or 70 per cent of Britain’s per capita GDP. {054-S07}
Instead, Shah said, we would have to hang our heads in shame and admit that India is a lower-middle-income coun­try at a tenth of the global fron­tier. The lit­er­acy came; the rest didn’t hap­pen.

quote.text: if you went back to Jawaharlal Nehru in a time ma­chine and said, 2024 we got like sev­enty-five per­cent lit­er­acy in India.

third.head: The test India ran from

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on India’s PISA retreat

body: India’s ed­u­ca­tion bu­reau­cracy long re­sisted the OECD’s PISA test, Ajay Shah said. That is par for the course for a state that likes to con­trol power and money with­out being ac­count­able for out­comes.
Under in­ter­na­tional pres­sure it al­lowed a lit­tle test­ing, and chose Himachal Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, “hop­ing that it would make India look good. And it didn’t.” {054-S03}
Their 15-year-olds came out among the worst in the world. As Shah re­mem­bers it, the bu­reau­cracy then ran away from the project and stopped mea­sur­ing. “So a cover up was pulled off,” he said.

There was one re­deem­ing fea­ture, an “upper tail bump” of re­mark­ably high scor­ers. Multiplied by India’s co­hort of 15-year-olds, it sug­gests the sec­ond or third largest plau­si­ble sci­en­tific and en­gi­neer­ing work­force in the world. {054-S04} The main­line, Shah said, is hor­ri­ble.

p2.deck: From Aser’s grim numbers to the first three years of life, the hosts’ case for fixing Indian education

quote.text: Fifty-seven per cent of kids in class five don’t un­der­stand what’s going on in class two.

box.title: The test that matters
box.text: The OECD’s PISA test, Ajay Shah said, sam­ples 15-year-olds from house­holds, not just schools, and tests whether they can apply sci­ence and math­e­mat­ics, not rote pro­ce­dures. Finland has the world’s high­est scores; South Korea and Japan do very well. {054-R11}

sections.label: The diagnosis
sections.head: Class five, reading class two
sections.caption: the state of Indian schooling
body: Every Indian knows in­tu­itively that the school sys­tem is a mess, Amit Varma said. What has changed in the twenty years he has been writ­ing about it is that there is now qual­ity data, and it says things are as bad as ever, or a lit­tle worse.
In Aser’s 2022 sur­vey, he said, 57 per cent of class five chil­dren could not read a class two text. {#aser57} For them, much of what is taught is “gob­bledy­gook”.
## Where the money goes
The usual rem­edy is to pump in more money. The Indian state al­ready spends about three per cent of GDP on ed­u­ca­tion, Varma said, mostly on salaries and build­ings. {#gdp}

Yet Karthik Muralidharan’s find­ings, he said, show that bet­ter build­ings, more toi­lets, “bet­ter” teach­ers and in­puts such as school bags do noth­ing for out­comes. Midday meals help in many other ways, but not with learn­ing.
The rea­son is the de­sign of the state. People put in the ef­fort until they are made per­ma­nent, Varma said, and “then they are chill­ing”. {#chilling}

Ajay Shah’s rem­edy be­gins with mea­sure­ment. Per pupil ex­pense, gov­ern­ment spend­ing di­vided by chil­dren in gov­ern­ment schools, has dou­bled and quadru­pled while out­comes have not im­proved. Without data, he said, “you can just thrash around for decades”. {054-C02}
~ Speaking as “a good or­tho­dox ex-Ministry of Finance per­son”, Shah said the coun­try would have done bet­ter by tak­ing all that money and pay­ing down debt. {054-J03}

quote.text: Fifty-seven per cent of kids in class five don’t un­der­stand what’s going on in class two.

sections.label: Private enterprise
sections.head: Profit, that dirty word
sections.caption: budget private schools
body: Jawaharlal Nehru fa­mously told JRD Tata not to speak to him of profit, as it was a dirty word. That at­ti­tude, Amit Varma said, lies be­hind the rule that schools can­not be run for profit. {054-J12}

The rule, Varma said, came from a mis­un­der­stand­ing of the profit mo­tive: “in a com­pet­i­tive mar­ket­place you earn a profit by serv­ing some­thing, in this case, serv­ing bet­ter ed­u­ca­tion.” {054-C04}
Then came li­cences, which Varma vaguely re­mem­bers num­ber­ing some forty-two to open a school in Delhi, and utopian rules on play­ground sizes and toi­lets. {#licences}
## The poor choose to pay

The poor pay any­way. James Tooley and Pauline Dixon found that many slum dwellers in Hyderabad chose bud­get pri­vate schools over free gov­ern­ment ones. {054-R05} A Centre for Civil Society sur­vey of poor Delhi house­holds found the same.

Outcomes, Varma said, are about the same or a lit­tle bet­ter in pri­vate schools, while gov­ern­ment schools spend three times as much per stu­dent. And par­ents can de­mand an­swers: “Where is a teacher?”
~ Varma’s model is 1991, when mar­kets were let into air­lines and tele­com and ac­cess ex­ploded. His plea, he said, is not to pri­va­tise ev­ery­thing, but to stop con­strain­ing pri­vate play­ers.

quote.text: Every par­ent wants their child to do bet­ter than they them­selves did to have op­por­tu­ni­ties they never had.

sections.label: The voucher
sections.head: Let the money follow the child
sections.caption: school vouchers
body: If the state will spend the money any­way, Amit Varma asked, how can it spend it bet­ter? His an­swer is to fund school­ing, not schools, through vouch­ers, an idea first pro­posed by Milton Friedman. {054-C06}

Parents would get a voucher worth what the state spends per child, to cash at any school, gov­ern­ment or pri­vate. Schools would then com­pete for stu­dents, and a teacher who stays ab­sent might find there is no job next year.
Varma’s lib­er­tar­ian friends say the state should spend noth­ing at all. His reply: don’t let the per­fect be the enemy of the good.
## Fairness per child
Ajay Shah went milder. Poor par­ents, he said, pay per­haps Rs 4,000 a year of their own money to leave a free gov­ern­ment school spend­ing about Rs 10,000 per pupil. {054-C05}
Let gov­ern­ment schools carry on, he said, but do not aban­don the chil­dren who leave. “Public spend­ing should be sym­met­ric per child.” {054-C07}
In his ad­vice to pol­i­cy­mak­ers, he rooted this in the Article 14 no­tion of equal­ity: spend per child in India, not per child in gov­ern­ment schools. {#article14}

~ The gov­ern­ment schools could be­come can­teens. A bell rings at noon, the chil­dren run over for the mid­day meal, and at 12:45 an­other bell sends them back. “So this is a great har­mo­nious co­ex­is­tence,” Shah said. {054-J04}

quote.text: Give it to the par­ents, let them de­cide. Let schools then have to com­pete.

sections.label: Education and growth
sections.head: Schools up, growth flat
sections.caption: Pritchett’s paradox
body: Amit Varma once as­sumed that a coun­try ed­u­cates its peo­ple first and de­vel­ops af­ter­wards. When told oth­er­wise, he re­sisted, until the data changed his mind more than a decade ago.
His friend Murali Neelakantan has mused that the link might run both ways, a vir­tu­ous cycle. Not so, Varma said: the cold hard data backs Lant Pritchett. {054-S06}

Ajay Shah set out the ev­i­dence. Pritchett’s 2001 paper, *Where Has All the Education Gone?*, was a cold sta­tis­ti­cal anal­y­sis across many coun­tries over long pe­ri­ods. Its an­swer, he said, was no gain at all. {054-R09}
Pritchett likes to note that Haiti’s ed­u­ca­tion mea­sures today are com­pa­ra­ble with France’s in 1970. France then was an ex­tremely de­vel­oped econ­omy; Haiti is deeply stuck. {054-J13}
## Three sus­pects

Shah of­fered three rival ex­pla­na­tions. Perhaps im­ple­men­ta­tion failed, which fits India but not the many coun­tries with de­cent gov­ern­ment schools. Perhaps ed­u­ca­tion is mostly sig­nalling, a Louis Vuitton bag. Or per­haps it is de­fined wrongly, fill­ing the pail in­stead of kin­dling the fire.
Varma backed the third. A sys­tem that tests a mon­key on how to climb a tree, he said, is also test­ing a fish on how to climb a tree. {054-J15}
~ The truth, Shah said, may lie in all three. Counting learn­ing out­comes in­stead of in­puts ex­plains part of the para­dox, but only part.

quote.text: Lant as he does so well was the child say­ing that the em­peror has no clothes, that all this mat­tered deadly squat.

sections.label: The early years
sections.head: Little ears, big conversations
sections.caption: the first five years
body: James Heckman, the University of Chicago econ­o­mist, spent his life ask­ing what works, with a hard-nosed eye on re­turn on in­vest­ment, Ajay Shah said. His an­swer is early child­hood, from birth to three or five, es­pe­cially for dis­ad­van­taged chil­dren. {054-R12}

Reading and arith­metic mat­ter, Shah said, and so do so­cial and emo­tional learn­ing and the reg­u­la­tion of be­hav­iour. From zero to three, he said, a child is adding a mil­lion neu­ral con­nec­tions every sec­ond. {054-C12}
## Overheard at home

Much of it comes from over­hear­ing. In a room where adults dis­cuss ideas with a rich vo­cab­u­lary, Shah said, chil­dren are “flap­ping their ears”. Heckman, half kid­ding, Shah thinks, once pro­posed pay­ing starv­ing grad­u­ate stu­dents to talk to dis­ad­van­taged chil­dren about ideas. {054-S08}

Family back­ground pre­dicts out­comes as strongly in wel­fare-state Denmark as in the United States, Shah said. Knowledge flows through fam­i­lies al­most un­no­ticed, which is why pop­ulist sneer­ing at nepo ba­bies misses the point. {054-C13}
Amit Varma called it an extra layer of priv­i­lege be­yond money. Miss those years, he said, and noth­ing can com­pen­sate.
~ Affluent Indian homes, Shah warned, are in­stead drenched in test prep or mass cul­ture. It was rain­ing on the out­door shoot, and Varma noted that they too were get­ting drenched.

quote.text: The fam­ily is a site where tremen­dous in­ter­gen­er­a­tional trans­for­ma­tion and knowl­edge flows take place.

sections.label: Advice to the young
sections.head: Don’t drink the Kool-Aid
sections.caption: credentialism and the young
body: Learning never ends, Ajay Shah said, not at grad­u­a­tion and not at a PhD. For the young, the great­est dan­ger is the Louis Vuitton bag of a fa­mous name: I’m from IIT, so I’m done.
“Don’t drink the Kool-Aid,” he said. Credentialism harms the cre­den­tialed first, mak­ing them com­pla­cent, and then cor­rupts how they judge ev­ery­one else. {054-C18}

Amit Varma added a nu­ance. Signalling and net­works are real, so take the IIT track if it is ra­tio­nal, but don’t be sin­gle-track. Immerse in sub­jects rather than flirt­ing with them. The for­mer cricket jour­nal­ist has stopped fol­low­ing the game: the IPL, he said, would take his evenings for a month and a half. {054-S12}
## Mixed ages, changed minds
Shah urged peo­ple to seek age het­ero­gene­ity. At 58, he counts a 25-year-old among the most im­por­tant peo­ple in his life. {054-C14}

And learn to change your mind. Dig in dur­ing an ar­gu­ment if you must, he said, but shift your views by five or ten per cent after a week’s re­flec­tion. “Actually that’s enough, you’re gold.” {054-C17}
~ Higher up the lad­der is thank­ing the per­son who changed your mind. Highest of all, Shah said, is say­ing “I was wrong”.

quote.text: If you’re a twenty-four year old sur­rounded by twenty-four year olds, you’re doing some­thing wrong.
I think it would be a darn good thing if par­ents un­der­stood that school is a day­care, that col­lege is day­care for teenagers, and no more. So do not con­fuse school with your ed­u­ca­tion.

p3.title: Tales out of school
p3.deck: Peons, local trains, scooters and orations at home: the stories behind the argument

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on degrees without skills
stories.head: The peon jobs PhDs queued for
body: Amit Varma sees the fail­ure of Indian ed­u­ca­tion most clearly in the job mar­ket. His friends who run com­pa­nies tell him they can­not find skilled peo­ple, which, he said, is why job-hopping is so com­mon in Bangalore. {#skilled}
Yet the coun­try also has what he called “a crazy un­em­ploy­ment prob­lem”, in which peo­ple with the high­est de­grees are not get­ting jobs. The two facts sit side by side.

The stark­est fig­ure came from Karthik Muralidharan, the guest on a mega episode of Varma’s other show, *The Seen and the Unseen*, who has writ­ten a re­cent book on the Indian state with a good chap­ter on ed­u­ca­tion.
There had been a re­cent ad­ver­tise­ment, Varma re­called, for 368 gov­ern­ment jobs at the level of a peon. About two and a half mil­lion peo­ple ap­plied, in­clud­ing 250 PhDs. {054-S01}
“Something to that ef­fect,” he added, care­ful with the fig­ures. By his reck­on­ing it came to some 6,500 ap­pli­cants for every peon’s post. “This is an in­cred­i­ble cri­sis.”

It is, Varma said, an il­lus­tra­tion of the fail­ure of the ed­u­ca­tion sys­tem “all the way through, not just in school”. A lot of de­grees, a lot of ed­u­ca­tion all the way up, is “not ac­tu­ally leav­ing you with any train­able skills”.
~ Nor is the gap only vo­ca­tional, he in­sisted. “You can’t un­der­stand the world. You can’t un­der­stand text. You’re not read­ing books,” he said. “This is a ter­ri­ble, ter­ri­ble prob­lem.”
stories.why: Mass un­em­ploy­ment and a short­age of skills can exist to­gether when de­grees are handed out with­out the abil­i­ties they claim to cer­tify. The fail­ure be­gins early: in class five, most chil­dren can­not read a class two text. {#aser57}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the 368 peon jobs

stories.head: First class, and a head taller
body: In the 1990s, when Amit Varma came to Bombay, he trav­elled by local train, and what he saw there was heart­break­ing.
People in first class were, on av­er­age, sig­nif­i­cantly taller than peo­ple in sec­ond class. A life­time of dif­fer­ent nu­tri­tion had writ­ten so­cial class onto their bod­ies. {054-S02}

The hosts had lamented be­fore, Varma said, that in India you can make out a person’s so­cial class from their height. {#heights} But height can be seen. “That is vis­i­ble, that is a seen,” he said. “What is un­seen is what the lack of ed­u­ca­tion also does to peo­ple.”
~ The dif­fer­ence in cog­ni­tive level, he said, is often stark. And that, he added, is a ter­ri­ble tragedy.

quote.text: it was heart­break­ing to see that the peo­ple in first class were on av­er­age sig­nif­i­cantly taller than the peo­ple in sec­ond class.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on heights in Bombay’s local trains

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah relays a theory from Josh Felman
stories.head: A pulpit in every home
body: Ajay Shah once asked Josh Felman why Jews have such out­sized in­tel­lec­tual achieve­ments, in­clud­ing the high­est num­ber of Nobel lau­re­ates per capita. {054-S09}

The stan­dard an­swer is se­lec­tion. In every gen­er­a­tion there was a pogrom, Shah said, and the peo­ple with por­ta­ble human cap­i­tal could up and move and flour­ish, while those who held land and phys­i­cal busi­nesses did not sur­vive as well.

Felman of­fered a dif­fer­ent ex­pla­na­tion. In the re­li­gious meet­ing, held at home rather than in a for­mal in­sti­tu­tion, it is not a priest who gives the ora­tion. The peo­ple do, each tak­ing a turn at a 10 to 15-minute talk that ties their per­sonal life to time­less prin­ci­ples.
~ “Every sin­gle per­son who went through that re­li­gious tra­di­tion was push­ing on this abil­ity,” Shah said. “Now that’s a high de­vel­op­ment of ca­pa­bil­ity.”
stories.why: When a cul­ture makes every or­di­nary mem­ber syn­the­sise ideas out loud, it builds ca­pa­bil­ity at scale. Shah praised se­ri­ous book clubs; Amit Varma re­called the Takshashila Institution’s Thursday rit­ual, where re­searchers present what they learned that week. {054-S10}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Josh Felman’s theory

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on planes and phones before 1991
stories.head: Daughter born? Book the scooter
body: Amit Varma is the son of an IAS of­fi­cer, yet he can­not re­call tak­ing a do­mes­tic flight as a child in the 1980s. “It was too much even for us,” he said. {054-S05}

The fam­ily flew only on a for­eign hol­i­day every three years or so. A phone line took five or six years. The joke, he re­called, was that when your daugh­ter is born you book a scooter, so that for her mar­riage it will be ready. {054-J05}
After the 1991 re­forms let mar­kets in, flights and phones be­came widely ac­ces­si­ble. Anybody can now get a phone in five min­utes, he said, and MTNL and BSNL are es­sen­tially ir­rel­e­vant.
~ In ed­u­ca­tion, which mat­ters most, India never let mar­kets in, Varma said.
stories.why: Where mar­kets were al­lowed, ac­cess ex­ploded. Varma does not want to pri­va­tise ev­ery­thing, he said, only to “just allow pri­vate forces to get into play and then see how things turn out”.

quiz.q: Which two states did India’s bureaucracy choose for PISA testing, hoping to look good?
quiz.a: Himachal Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, whose 15-year-olds ranked among the world’s worst.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s usage, what does PPE stand for, if not protective equipment?
quiz.a: Per pupil ex­pense: gov­ern­ment school spend­ing di­vided by chil­dren en­rolled in gov­ern­ment schools.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah propose government schools should become, once children move to private ones?
quiz.a: Canteens run­ning the mid­day meal, with bells ring­ing at noon and 12:45.

quiz.q: Which single personality trait, according to Shah, does industrial schooling measure and nurture?
quiz.a: Conscientiousness, so the chil­dren who take or­ders and obey are the ones who flour­ish.

quiz.q: What did Shah call the world’s most effective use of philanthropic capital ever?
quiz.a: The fund­ing that went to Aser, which changed how think­ing peo­ple see el­e­men­tary ed­u­ca­tion.

glossary.def: Judging peo­ple, your­self in­cluded, by de­grees rather than by abil­ity.
An un­usual clus­ter of very high scor­ers at a distribution’s top.
Education as a badge that sorts peo­ple rather than teach­ing them.
A bu­reau­crat; old-style schools were de­signed to churn them out.
Curd; an in­te­grated mind thinks bet­ter even about mak­ing it.
An of­fice at­ten­dant; 368 such gov­ern­ment posts drew 2.5 mil­lion ap­pli­cants.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 54. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: James Heckman (Andreas Caranti, CC BY-SA 3.0); JRD Tata (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain); Harper Lee (Eric Draper, public domain); Lydia Davis (kellywritershouse, CC BY 2.0).

shelf.title: The Collected Stories of Lydia Davis
shelf.creator: Lydia Davis
shelf.why: Fiction lets you enter the minds of oth­ers and live their lives.

shelf.title: Essays
shelf.creator: Lydia Davis
shelf.why: Davis writ­ing about her own craft and lit­er­a­ture, ‘and much more besides’.

shelf.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
shelf.creator: Harper Lee
shelf.why: Ajay read it grow­ing up as a mas­ter­piece about a par­ent and child fac­ing big­otry he as­sumed was in the past; now he finds it a hun­dred times more rel­e­vant.

shelf.title: The Beautiful Tree
shelf.creator: James Tooley
shelf.why: A ‘won­der­ful book’ on bud­get pri­vate schools serv­ing the poor, grounded in work among poor fam­i­lies and how they ac­tu­ally choose.

shelf.title: Private Education Is Good for the Poor
shelf.creator: James Tooley and Pauline Dixon
shelf.why: Their Hyderabad study found many slum dwellers chose to pay for bud­get pri­vate schools over free gov­ern­ment ones.

shelf.title: How Much Does Free Education Cost?
shelf.creator: Centre for Civil Society
shelf.why: A Delhi sur­vey of house­holds earn­ing under Rs 5,000 a month found the same thing: a large share send their kids to bud­get pri­vate schools.

shelf.title: The Aser Reports
shelf.creator: Aser Centre
shelf.why: Simple mea­sure­ment of learn­ing done at scale every year.

shelf.title: Accelerating India’s Development
shelf.creator: Karthik Muralidharan
shelf.why: Karthik Muralidharan’s book is the source of strik­ing facts the hosts use: the av­er­age dis­trict is big­ger than 85 coun­tries, only 3% of India’s bud­get is spent lo­cally against 50% in China, and more spend­ing on build­ings, school bags or ‘better’ teach­ers does noth­ing for learn­ing out­comes.

shelf.title: Where Has All the Education Gone?
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: Pritchett’s cross-country anal­y­sis find­ing that ex­pand­ing school­ing pro­duced es­sen­tially zero growth, which Ajay calls one of the most im­por­tant pa­pers in de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics.

shelf.title: The first PISA results for India: The end of the beginning
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: Pritchett on what India’s first PISA re­sults re­vealed.

shelf.title: PISA
shelf.creator: OECD
shelf.why: It tests a house­hold-based ran­dom sam­ple of 15-year-olds, not just those in school, on ap­ply­ing sci­ence and maths rather than rote mem­ory.

shelf.title: James Heckman’s work on early childhood / The Heckman Equation
shelf.creator: James Heckman
shelf.why: Hard-nosed re­turn-on-investment ev­i­dence that the big­gest pay­offs come from in­ter­ven­tions at ages 0 to 5, es­pe­cially for dis­ad­van­taged chil­dren: hear­ing com­plex ‘ten-letter words’ early builds a layer of in­tel­li­gence that can’t be made up later.

shelf.title: Google Scholar’s citations list
shelf.why: Open any paper, click its ci­ta­tion count, and you see every later paper that en­gaged with it, both crit­ics and fol­low-ups.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s long-form pod­cast of three-to-eight-hour deep dives, con­ver­sa­tions no gate­keeper would have com­mis­sioned, which have be­come an oral his­tory of India; its show notes list every book men­tioned.

shelf.title: Natasha Badhwar Lives the Examined Life (Episode 301, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Natasha Badhwar, who home­schools her chil­dren, on par­ent­ing, writ­ing and how to ed­u­cate your kids; Amit calls it his ‘per­fect episode’ for its bal­ance and a gen­er­ous guest.

shelf.title: The Takshashila Institution
shelf.why: Its weekly rit­ual of re­searchers pre­sent­ing what they learned that week is Amit’s liv­ing ex­am­ple of mul­ti­dis­ci­plinary group learn­ing.

shelf.title: Fixing Indian Education (Episode 185, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A deep dive with Karthik Muralidharan into what’s bro­ken in Indian ed­u­ca­tion and how to fix it, in­clud­ing his point that the sys­tem is op­ti­mised for sort­ing, not teach­ing.

shelf.title: Karthik Muralidharan and the Bureaucrat’s Burden (Episode 375, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Gives Muralidharan’s side of the de­bate, in which fo­cus­ing on ed­u­ca­tion was im­plied to be the route to de­vel­op­ment.

shelf.title: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A deep con­ver­sa­tion with Lant Pritchett on why growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion, drives human wel­fare, why causal­ity runs from de­vel­op­ment to ed­u­ca­tion, and why many RCTs solve small mea­sur­able prob­lems in­stead of mov­ing the nee­dle on poverty.

shelf.title: Education in India (Episode 77, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: An ear­lier long-form con­ver­sa­tion with Amit Chandra on the state of Indian ed­u­ca­tion, an­other field the hosts say suf­fers from keep­ing prices out.

shelf.title: We Are Brains, Not Stomachs (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The ar­gu­ment that peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs: hu­mans are in­no­va­tors whose cre­ativ­ity beats scarcity, so India’s prob­lem is too few chil­dren and too lit­tle train­ing of minds, not too many peo­ple.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Episode 46, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: On be­liefs im­ported from rich-world dis­course that make their hold­ers feel vir­tu­ous while hurt­ing the peo­ple they claim to help, such as the min­i­mum wage, or op­pos­ing sweat­shops that beat every other op­tion work­ers have.

shelf.title: Why India Needs School Vouchers
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: His early case for school vouch­ers, the episode’s main pro­posal for spend­ing pub­lic money bet­ter.

shelf.title: Fund Schooling, Not Schools
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The core voucher idea: pub­lic money should fol­low the child to what­ever school the par­ent chooses.

shelf.title: Our Unlucky Children
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that mar­kets give us forty flavours of potato chips and a thou­sand sham­poos while ed­u­ca­tion stays one-size-fits-all, built in the 19th cen­tury to pro­duce work­ers, be­cause mar­kets aren’t al­lowed to work there.

shelf.title: It is immoral to have children. Here’s why
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s de­lib­er­ately provoca­tive col­umn: we agree not to act on peo­ple with­out con­sent, cause pain or kill, yet a child is born with­out con­sent and will suf­fer and die.

shelf.title: Geniuses and economic development
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ties to the idea that India’s small but, in ab­so­lute num­bers, huge pool of very ca­pa­ble peo­ple mat­ters for de­vel­op­ment.

shelf.title: Doing better than a competitive exam
shelf.creator: Nitin Pai and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Nitin Pai and Ajay’s case against or­gan­is­ing Indian ed­u­ca­tion around sin­gle exams like UPSC, IIT-JEE and the boards, with a pro­posal: a con­cep­tual exam to qual­ify the top one lakh stu­dents, then a lot­tery for IIT seats.

shelf.title: Three page notes considered harmful
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It de­scribes the pathol­ogy: a half-baked idea, a three-page note, three prac­ti­tion­ers con­sulted, no thinkers at the table, and then a bad idea gets im­ple­mented.

laughs.text: Right after Ajay ex­plains the ‘upper tail bump’ in India’s PISA dis­tri­bu­tion, Amit says: ‘You’re look­ing very hot today. Can I give you an upper tail bump?’

Ajay’s plan for gov­ern­ment schools: turn them into can­teens. Kids study at pri­vate schools, a bell rings at noon, they run to the gov­ern­ment school for the mid­day meal, and at 12:45 an­other bell sends them run­ning back. ‘So this is a great har­mo­nious co­ex­is­tence.’

Ajay im­i­tat­ing a cre­den­tial snob: ‘Oh, this Amit guy, he doesn’t par­tic­u­larly have any de­grees. He doesn’t have that Louis Vuitton bag. So he must be a clue­less bug­ger.’ Amit later: ‘this man here went to IIT, this man here went abroad and got fancy PhD. This man here has no cre­den­tials what­so­ever. We can still be friends, right?’
Nehru’s fa­mous line to JRD Tata, ‘do not speak to me of profit. It is a dirty word’, cited by Amit as the root of the ban on for-profit ed­u­ca­tion.

Amit on one-size-fits-all school­ing: ‘If you’re going to test a mon­key on how to climb a tree, you’re also test­ing a fish on how to climb a tree.’ He con­trasts it with su­per­mar­kets of­fer­ing forty types of ketchup and thirty types of ghee.
